title: the one behind your eyes
hook: what stays when everything else about you changes
tomorrow: the ocean the wave forgets it is

segments.voice: Yesterday: karma. Your line was what you do, you become. Did you plant one thing on purpose? Today we turn from what gets done to the one doing it. Day ten.

A question with no trick in it. Who is hearing this sentence? Not what. Who. The quick answer is: me. But try pointing at the me. The body? It has been changing since childhood. The mood? It may have shifted twice since breakfast. The thoughts? They're moving faster than this voice. Everything you can point to keeps moving. And yet, the Upanishads say, something has been there for all of it, the one all of it happened to. A teacher in an old Hindu text was pressed on exactly this, and his answer turned the question around. Today's word is what he was pointing at.
screen: `WHO IS HEARING THIS?` → `NOT THE BODY. NOT THE MOOD.` → `SOMETHING HAS BEEN THERE FOR ALL OF IT.`

segments.voice: Atman. The self. Not the self in selfie, the personality you show the world. The Upanishads use atman for the deepest you: the one that is aware. And they notice something strange about it. You can't look straight at it. In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, a questioner keeps pressing the teacher Yajnavalkya: show me this self, plainly, the way you'd point and say, that's a cow, that's a horse. And Yajnavalkya answers, in effect: you can't see the seer of seeing. You can't hear the hearer of hearing. The one who looks can't become one more thing on the table to be looked at. So, in other passages, the same Upanishad describes the self by saying what it is not: neti, neti. Not this, not this. Whatever you can point to, the body, the breath, the busy mind, the self is not that. One way to put the Upanishad's point: take away everything that can be watched, and what's left is the watching. Put plainly: someone is in there. Today that someone gets its name. Here's where it turns practical. When worry comes, it comes as something seen: a thought, a tight chest, a story about tomorrow. The Upanishad points past it, to the one who sees. Hindu schools describe the atman in different ways. Some teach that the self is one with the whole. Others teach that it is a distinct soul, forever dear to God and dependent on God. Tomorrow brings the word for the whole. Today, just the turn this word makes: away from what's being watched, toward the one who is watching.
screen: `ATMAN — THE SELF THAT IS AWARE` · `THE SEER OF SEEING` · `NETI, NETI — NOT THIS, NOT THIS` · `THE WATCHING, NOT THE WATCHED` · then, large: `SOMEONE IS IN THERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice the noticer. Sit and breathe. Let a thought arrive, any thought. Don't follow it. Just see that it's there. Now notice that something saw it. Rest there for a moment, not in the thought, in the seeing. Another thought will come; that's what thoughts do. Same move: see it, then notice the one who saw. No need to get anywhere. The bell holds the time.
Atman. The self: not the body, not the thoughts, but the one aware of them. Tenth word.
Your line: someone is in there. When worry shows up today, ask once, quietly: who is seeing this? Just the question. Day ten.

screen: `DAY 10 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE OCEAN THE WAVE FORGETS IT IS.`

howItsDone: Hindus who follow the Upanishads study the self through teachers and texts, and in meditation and self-inquiry turn attention from thoughts to the one who is aware of them; schools differ on how the self relates to God.

original.note: Sanskrit: the self, the inner one who is aware.

trapdoor: what you thought: the self is your personality, or a ghost inside the body.
what it means: the self that is aware: not the body, not the thoughts, the one who sees them.
what a scholar hears: Brihadaranyaka 3.4.2, you can't see the seer of seeing; and its refrain, sa esha neti neti atma: this self is not this, not this.

notes: Editor pass (days 8–14): hook no longer says Yajnavalkya's answer to Ushasta was 'two words, said twice' (neti neti is one word twice, and it comes from other passages, BU 3.9.26 / 4.2.4, not the 3.4 exchange); 'neti, neti' now introduced as 'in other passages'; Ushasta called a questioner, not a student; the narrator's 'something has been there for all of it' attributed to the Upanishads; practice's 'if you pray' line dropped to vary the week's practice closes.

Written from the camp-one manuscript day 10 under the claims rule: the manuscript's 'every cell replaced', 'three thousand years old' and 'the oldest texts' were cut; the hook calls the Brihadaranyaka 'an old Hindu text'.
BU 3.4.2: the questioner is Ushasta Cakrayana; the 'point to it like a cow or a horse' image and 'you cannot see the seer of seeing' (na drishter drashtaram pashyeh) are paraphrased. Confirm.
Refrain 'sa esha neti neti atma' quoted in the trapdoor (BU 3.9.26 and parallels); confirm transliteration.
Schools: 'one with the whole' (Advaita) and 'a distinct soul, forever dear to God and dependent on God' (Dvaita, and in its own way Vishishtadvaita). Confirm the summary is fair.

Audit (2026-10-01): 'take away everything that can be watched, what's left is the watching' reframed as one way to put the point (it leans Advaita, and the teach goes on to say schools differ); carry reworded because 'when something rattles you today' repeated day 4's carry. BU 3.4.2 (Ushasta, cow/horse image, seer of seeing) and neti neti references checked.
